facts.statement: Psittacosaurus lived between 125 and 105 million years ago.
facts.quote: existing between 125 and 105 million years ago

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus is the most species-rich non-avian dinosaur genus, with up to 13 known species.
facts.quote: It is notable for being the most species-rich non-avian dinosaur genus. Up to 13 species are known

facts.statement: Adult Psittacosaurus were obligate bipeds characterized by a high skull and a robust beak.
facts.quote: The species of Psittacosaurus were obligate bipeds at adulthood, with a high skull and a robust beak

facts.statement: One Psittacosaurus individual was preserved with long filaments on its tail, similar to those found in Tianyulong.
facts.quote: One individual was found preserved with long filaments on the tail, similar to those of Tianyulong

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus likely had well-developed senses of smell and vision and may have been active for short periods during both day and night.
facts.quote: It may have been active for short periods of time during the day and night, and had well-developed senses of smell and vision

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus was once placed in its own family, Psittacosauridae, but is now considered the senior synonym of Hongshanosaurus.
facts.quote: Once in its own family, Psittacosauridae, with other genera like Hongshanosaurus, it is now considered to be senior synonym of the latter

facts.statement: Henry Fairfield Osborn participated in the Third Asiatic Expedition of the American Museum of Natural History in 1922 to discover fossils in Mongolia.
facts.quote: In 1922, American paleontologist Henry Fairfield Osborn took part in the Third Asiatic Expedition of the American Museum of Natural History to discover fossils and geologic formations from the Cretaceous and Tertiary of Mongolia

facts.statement: The specimen catalogued as AMNH 6254 was described in 1924 by Osborn and named Psittacosaurus mongoliensis.
facts.quote: The specimen, catalogued as AMNH 6254, was described in 1924 by Osborn, only partially prepared, who gave it the name Psittacosaurus mongoliensis

facts.statement: Osborn distinguished Psittacosaurus by its short and deep snout, broad rear skull, and lack of teeth in the premaxilla.
facts.quote: Osborn demonstrated the taxon was unique based on the short and deep snout, and the broad rear skull, as well as by lacking teeth in the premaxilla

facts.statement: Osborn established the family Psittacosauridae for Psittacosaurus, considering it possibly related to Ankylosauria.
facts.quote: Osborn created the new family Psittacosauridae for Psittacosaurus, which he considered possibly related to Ankylosauria

facts.statement: William King Gregory suggested that the Protiguanodon specimen might be a juvenile Psittacosaurus based on similarities in size, parietal bones, and quadrate bones.
facts.quote: Gregory suggested in correspondence that the Protiguanodon specimen could represent a juvenile of Psittacosaurus, based on similarities in size, the parietal bones, and the quadrate bones

facts.statement: Yang Zhongjian described two additional Psittacosaurus species in 1932 following the discovery of material in Haratologay, Inner Mongolia.
facts.quote: Following the discovery of material of psittacosaurids in Haratologay in Inner Mongolia, Yang Zhongjian described two additional species in 1932

facts.statement: Birger Bohlin described additional Psittacosaurus material in 1953, considering the remains likely belonged to P. mongoliensis.
facts.quote: Additional Psittacosaurus material from possibly the same locality was described later in 1953 by Birger Bohlin, who considered the remains to likely belong to P. mongoliensis

facts.statement: Fossils of Psittacosaurus have been found across China, Mongolia, Russia, and Thailand.
facts.quote: from across China, Mongolia, Russia, and Thailand

facts.statement: The abundance of Psittacosaurus fossils has led to the designation of Lower Cretaceous sediments in East Asia as the Psittacosaurus biochron.
facts.quote: The abundance of this dinosaur in the fossil record has led to the labelling of Lower Cretaceous sediments of east Asia the Psittacosaurus biochron

facts.statement: The discovery location is known as the Oshih locality within the Khukhtek Formation, dating to the Early Cretaceous Aptian to Albian age.
facts.quote: The location of discovery is also known as the Oshih locality of the Khukhtek Formation, of Early Cretaceous Aptian to Albian age

facts.statement: Soviet expeditions discovered additional Psittacosaurus fossils in Mongolia between 1946 and 1949.
facts.quote: The Soviet Expeditions into Mongolia from 1946 to 1949 uncovered more material of Psittacosaurus.

facts.statement: A disarticulated specimen of Psittacosaurus mongoliensis was found at the Ulan Osh locality in 1946.
facts.quote: In 1946 they discovered a new locality, Ulan Osh, where a disarticulated specimen of Psittacosaurus mongoliensis was found

facts.statement: Soviet excavations near Kemerovo in Siberia uncovered a partial skull and skeleton belonging to multiple Psittacosaurus individuals.
facts.quote: Soviet excavations near Kemerovo in Siberia also discovered a partial skull and skeleton of multiple individuals referrable to Psittacosaurus.

facts.statement: Soviet paleontologist Anatoly Rozhdestvensky described the Siberian Psittacosaurus material in 1955.
facts.quote: This material was described by Soviet paleontologist Anatoly Rozhdestvensky in 1955

facts.statement: Yang described multiple Psittacosaurus discoveries from the Qingshan Formation in Laiyang in a 1958 paper.
facts.quote: In 1958, Yang published a paper on the dinosaurs of Laiyang, in which he described multiple discoveries of Psittacosaurus from a collection of localities of the Qingshan Formation.

facts.statement: Yang assigned 11 other specimens to Psittacosaurus sinensis, considering it the most diverse species known at that time.
facts.quote: Yang also assigned 11 other specimens to the taxon, considering it to be the most diverse Psittacosaurus species known at the time.

facts.statement: Zhao Xijin described a 1958 discovery from Laiyang in 1962, naming it Psittacosaurus youngi based on specimen BPV.149.
facts.quote: Further discoveries in the Qingshan Formation of Laiyang in 1958 were described by Zhao Xijin in 1962, giving the new name Psittacosaurus youngi for the specimen BPV.149 in the Beijing Museum of Natural History.

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus youngi is known for having the shortest skull, vertebral series, and tooth counts among all species.
facts.quote: Known for a complete skull, partial vertebral series and partial pelvis, P. youngi was distinguished by Zhao by having the shortest skull of all species, vertebral and tooth counts, and various features of the skull and skeleton.

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus mongoliensis fossils date to the Aptian to Albian stages of the Early Cretaceous, approximately 125 to 100 million years ago.
facts.quote: In these areas, Psittacosaurus mongoliensis fossils are found in most sedimentary strata dating to the Aptian to Albian stages of the Early Cretaceous Period, or approximately 125 to 100 mya.

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus individuals ranged from hatchlings under 13 cm long to adults nearly 2 meters long.
facts.quote: Individuals of all ages are known, from hatchlings less than 13 cm long, to very old adults reaching nearly 2 m in length.

facts.statement: In 2010, Sereno tentatively regarded P. osborni as a synonym of P. mongoliensis due to the presence of other valid psittacosaur species in Inner Mongolia.
facts.quote: In a 2010 review, Sereno again regarded P. osborni as a synonym of P. mongoliensis, but noted it was tentative because of the presence of multiple valid psittacosaur species in Inner Mongolia.

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus sinensis was distinguished by a shorter and wider snout and a smaller size of 675 mm.
facts.quote: Yang also assigned 11 other specimens to the taxon, considering it to be the most diverse Psittacosaurus species known at the time. It was distinguished from the other known species by a shorter and wider snout, and an overall smaller size at 675 mm.

facts.statement: The genus Psittacosaurus includes seventeen referred species, though only nine to eleven are currently considered valid.
facts.quote: Seventeen species have been referred to the genus Psittacosaurus, although only nine to eleven are considered valid today.

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus holds the record for the highest number of valid species assigned to any single non-avian dinosaur genus.
facts.quote: This is the highest number of valid species currently assigned to any single non-avian dinosaur.

facts.statement: The species P. sinensis was discovered in the 1950s in the Aptian-Albian Qingshan Formation of Shandong Province, southeast of Beijing.
facts.quote: In the 1950s, a new Chinese species of Psittacosaurus was found in the Aptian-Albian Qingshan Formation of Shandong Province, southeast of Beijing.

facts.statement: C. C. Young named the species P. sinensis to differentiate it from P. mongoliensis, which was originally found in Mongolia.
facts.quote: C. C. Young called it P. sinensis to differentiate it from P. mongoliensis, which had originally been found in Mongolia.

facts.statement: Chinese paleontologist Zhao Xijin named the species P. youngi in 1962 after his mentor, C. C. Young.
facts.quote: Chinese paleontologist Zhao Xijin named a new species after his mentor, C. C. Young, in 1962.

facts.statement: Zhao and Paul Sereno described P. xinjiangensis in 1988, naming it after the Xinjiang Autonomous Region where it was found.
facts.quote: In 1988, Zhao and American paleontologist Paul Sereno described P. xinjiangensis, named after the Xinjiang Autonomous Region in which it was discovered.

facts.statement: Several individuals of P. xinjiangensis were discovered in the early 1970s, with the holotype and most complete skeleton belonging to a juvenile.
facts.quote: Several individuals of different ages were discovered in the early 1970s by Chinese paleontologists and described by Sereno and Zhao, although the holotype and most complete skeleton belonged to a juvenile.

facts.statement: Specimens of P. xinjiangensis come from the upper part of the Tugulu Group, which is dated to the Aptian-Albian age.
facts.quote: These specimens come from the upper part of the Tugulu Group, which is regarded as Aptian-Albian in age.

facts.statement: P. meileyingensis was described in 1988 by Sereno, Zhao, and two Chinese colleagues from the Jiufotang Formation near Meileyingzi in Liaoning Province.
facts.quote: A second species described in 1988 by Sereno and Zhao, along with two Chinese colleagues, was P. meileyingensis from the Jiufotang Formation, near the town of Meileyingzi, Liaoning Province, northeastern China.

facts.statement: P. meileyingensis is known from four fossil skulls and one associated skeleton found in 1973 by Chinese scientists.
facts.quote: This species is known from four fossil skulls, one associated with some skeletal material, found in 1973 by Chinese scientists.

facts.statement: While the age of the Jiufotang Formation in Liaoning is unknown, the neighboring Inner Mongolia province dates it to about 110 million years ago in the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: The age of the Jiufotang in Liaoning is unknown, but in the neighbouring province of Inner Mongolia, it has been dated to about 110 Ma, in the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Eric Buffetaut and Varavudh Suteethorn described P. sattayaraki in 1992 based on a partial jaw from the Aptian-Albian Khok Kruat Formation of Thailand.
facts.quote: French paleontologist Eric Buffetaut and a Thai colleague, Varavudh Suteethorn, described a partial upper and lower jaw from the Aptian-Albian Khok Kruat Formation of Thailand in 1992, giving it the name P. sattayaraki.

facts.statement: Paul Sereno questioned the validity of P. sattayaraki in 2000 due to its eroded, fragmentary nature and lack of characteristic Psittacosaurus features.
facts.quote: In 2000, Sereno questioned the validity of this species, citing its eroded and fragmentary nature, and noted an absence of features characteristic of the genus Psittacosaurus.

facts.statement: In 2002, the original authors of P. sattayaraki published new images showing teeth with a bulbous vertical ridge characteristic of psittacosaurs, defending the species' validity.
facts.quote: However, in 2002 the original authors published new images of the fossil which seem to show teeth in the lower jaw that exhibit the bulbous vertical ridge characteristic of psittacosaurs.

facts.statement: In 2010, Paul Sereno proposed that the type material of P. sattayaraki might best be assigned to Ceratopsia incertae sedis.
facts.quote: Sereno (2010) proposed that the best assignment for the type material may be Ceratopsia incertae sedis.

facts.statement: Canadian paleontologist Dale Russell and Zhao described two new species of Psittacosaurus in 1996.
facts.quote: Two new species of Psittacosaurus were described by Canadian Dale Russell and Zhao in 1996.

facts.statement: P. neimongoliensis was named after Inner Mongolia and is based on a nearly complete skeleton found in the Early Cretaceous Ejinhoro Formation along with seven other individuals.
facts.quote: The first was named P. neimongoliensis, after the Mandarin Chinese name for Inner Mongolia. It is based on a nearly complete fossil skeleton, including most of the skull, found in the Early Cretaceous Ejinhoro Formation with seven other individuals.

facts.statement: P. ordosensis was named in 1996 after the Ordos prefecture in the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region.
facts.quote: Russell and Zhao also named P. ordosensis in 1996, after the Ordos prefecture of the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region.

facts.statement: Paul Sereno found P. ordosensis indistinguishable from P. sinensis in 2010 but suggested further study might reveal diagnostic features.
facts.quote: Sereno (2010) found the species as described to be indistinguishable from P. sinensis, another small species, but suggested that additional study of P. ordosensis might reveal diagnostic features.

facts.statement: Paul Sereno provisionally designated P. ordosensis as a nomen dubium.
facts.quote: He provisionally designated P. ordosensis a nomen dubium.

facts.statement: In 1997, Chinese paleontologist Xu Xing named a new species of Psittacosaurus based on a complete skull, vertebrae, and a forelimb.
facts.quote: Xu Xing, another Chinese paleontologist, named a new species of Psittacosaurus in 1997, based on a complete skull with associated vertebrae and a forelimb.

facts.statement: Remains of P. mazongshanensis were found in the Lower Xinminbao Formation, likely deposited during the late Barremian to Aptian stages.
facts.quote: The remains were found in the Lower Xinminbao Formation, which have not been precisely dated, although there is some evidence that they were deposited in the late Barremian through Aptian stages.

facts.statement: In 2000, Sereno suggested that P. mazongshanensis was a nomen dubium because it lacked unique features separating it from other Psittacosaurus species.
facts.quote: Sereno suggested in 2000 that P. mazongshanensis was a nomen dubium, with no unique features that separate it from any other species of Psittacosaurus.

facts.statement: P. sibiricus remains, including two nearly complete skeletons, were found in the Ilek Formation of Siberia, dating from the Barremian to Aptian stages of the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: The remains were not completely described until 2006. Two nearly complete, articulated skeletons and a variety of disarticulated material from other individuals of all ages are known from the Ilek Formation of Siberia, which ranges from the Barremian to Aptian stages of the Early Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Revised dating methods indicate that the Yixian Formation beds containing P. lujiatunensis are approximately 123 million years old.
facts.quote: While this bed has been dated differently by different authors, from 128 Ma in the Barremian stage, to 125 Ma in the earliest Aptian, revised dating methods have shown them to be about 123 million years old.

facts.statement: Sereno (2010) considered P. lujiatunensis and H. houi to be separate species due to inadequacies in the type specimen of H. houi, despite proposing that Hongshanosaurus is a synonym of Psittacosaurus.
facts.quote: It is potentially synonymous with H. houi; Sereno (2010), who proposed that Hongshanosaurus is a synonym of Psittacosaurus, opted to leave P. lujiatunensis and H. houi separate species due to the inadequacies of the latter's type specimen.

facts.statement: P. major was originally characterized by a skull that was 39% of the torso length, compared to 30% in P. mongoliensis.
facts.quote: P. major was originally characterised by a proportionately large skull, which was 39% of the length of its torso, compared to 30% in P. mongoliensis, and other features.

facts.statement: A 2013 study concluded that differences between P. lujiatunensis and P. major were due to preservation and crushing, suggesting they represent a single species.
facts.quote: However, a 2013 study utilising morphometric analysis showed that the supposed differences between P. lujiatunensis and P. major were due to differences in preservation and crushing. The study concluded that both represented a single species.

facts.statement: Hongshanosaurus houi was first named in 2003, with the generic name derived from Chinese words for 'red' and 'hill' and the Greek word for 'lizard'.
facts.quote: A third species of Lujiatun psittacosaur, the first to be named, was described as Hongshanosaurus houi in 2003. The generic name Hongshanosaurus was derived from the Mandarin Chinese words 紅 (hóng: "red") and 山 (shān: "hill"), as well as the Greek word sauros ("lizard").

facts.statement: The genus and species Hongshanosaurus houi were named in 2003 by You Hailu, Xu Xing, and Wang Xiaolin.
facts.quote: Genus and species were both named by Chinese paleontologists You Hailu, Xu Xing, and Wang Xiaolin in 2003.

facts.statement: Sereno (2010) regarded Hongshanosaurus as a junior synonym of Psittacosaurus, potentially the same as P. lujiatunensis, attributing distinct proportions to skull crushing.
facts.quote: Sereno (2010) regarded its distinct proportions as due to crushing and compression of the Hongshanosaurus skulls. He regarded Hongshanosaurus as a junior synonym of Psittacosaurus, and potentially the same as P. lujiatunensis.

facts.statement: P. gobiensis was first described by Sereno, Zhao, and Lin in 2010, named for the region where it was found in 2001.
facts.quote: P. gobiensis is named for the region it was found in 2001, and first described by Sereno, Zhao and Lin in 2010.

facts.statement: P. gobiensis is known from a skull and partial skeleton that includes gastroliths.
facts.quote: It is known from a skull and partial articulated skeleton with gastroliths.

facts.statement: Nearly 100 Psittacosaurus skeletons were excavated in Mongolia in 2005 and 2006 by a team led by Bolortsetseg Minjin and Jack Horner.
facts.quote: Nearly 100 Psittacosaurus skeletons were excavated in Mongolia during the summers of 2005 and 2006 by a team led by Mongolian paleontologist Bolortsetseg Minjin and American Jack Horner from the Museum of the Rockies in Montana.

facts.statement: P. amitabha was named in 2019 by James Napoli and colleagues based on a nearly complete skull, mandibles, and fragmentary postcranial skeleton.
facts.quote: P. amitabha was named by American researcher James Napoli and colleagues in 2019 from a nearly complete skull, mandibles and a fragmentary postcranial skeleton.

facts.statement: P. amitabha is one of the few vertebrate fossils from the Andakhuduk Formation, which dates to the Barremian stage of the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: This specimen is one of the few vertebrate fossils known from the Andakhuduk Formation, which dates to the Barremian stage of the early Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: The best-known species, P. mongoliensis, could reach a length of 2 meters (6.5 feet).
facts.quote: The best-known—P. mongoliensis—can reach 2 metres (6.5 ft) in length.

facts.statement: The maximum adult body weight of P. mongoliensis was likely over 20 kilograms (44 pounds).
facts.quote: The maximum adult body weight was most likely over 20 kilogrammes (44 lb) in P. mongoliensis.

facts.statement: The portion of the skull in front of the eye socket is only 40% of the total skull length, which is shorter than in any other known ornithischian.
facts.quote: The portion in front of the orbit (eye socket) is only 40% of total skull length, shorter than any other known ornithischian.

facts.statement: Bony horns are found on the skull of P. sibiricus, but scientists believe they resulted from convergent evolution.
facts.quote: Bony horns protrude from the skull of P. sibiricus, but these are thought to be an example of convergent evolution.

facts.statement: A row of hollow, tubular bristle-like structures approximately 16 centimeters long was preserved along the upper surface of the tail.
facts.quote: A series of what appear to be hollow, tubular bristle-like structures, approximately 16 cm long, were also preserved, arranged in a row down the dorsal (upper) surface of the tail.

facts.statement: The collagen tissue fibers in Psittacosaurus have an exceptional thickness of about forty layers compared to other vertebrates.
facts.quote: The collagen tissue fibres in Psittacosaurus are complex, virtually identical to all other vertebrates in structure but having an exceptional thickness of about forty layers.

facts.statement: Analysis of preserved melanosomes indicates that Psittacosaurus was countershaded.
facts.quote: examination of melanosomes preserved in the specimen of Psittacosaurus preserved with integument indicated that the animal was countershaded

facts.statement: The specimen had dense pigment clusters on its shoulders, face, and cloaca.
facts.quote: The specimen also had dense clusters of pigment on its shoulders, face (possibly for display), and cloaca

facts.statement: Large eyes suggest Psittacosaurus had good vision useful for finding food or avoiding predators.
facts.quote: Its large eyes indicate that it also likely had good vision, which would have been useful in finding food or avoiding predators.

facts.statement: A 2022 study identified a specimen as a 6–7 year old subadult and found it preserves the first known umbilicus from a non-avian dinosaur.
facts.quote: A 2022 study of SMF R 4970 identified it as an approximately 6–7 year old subadult by comparing its femoral length to that of similarly-aged specimens of P. lujiatunensis, and found that it preserves the first umbilicus (belly button) known from a non-avian dinosaur

facts.statement: Studies state there is currently no convincing evidence that the tail bristles are homologous to the integumentary filaments of theropod dinosaurs.
facts.quote: The study stated that, "at present, there is no convincing evidence which shows these structures to be homologous to the structurally different integumentary filaments of theropod dinosaurs".

facts.statement: A 2016 study concluded that the tail structures were highly modified scales rather than feathers due to their morphology and anatomy.
facts.quote: A 2016 study by Ji Qiang and colleagues was published in the Journal of Geology. Their conclusion was that these were actually highly modified scales because the morphology and anatomy did not resemble feathers.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the pigment clusters on the cloaca served an antimicrobial function.
facts.quote: which may have had an antimicrobial function, though this has been disputed

facts.statement: The skull of Psittacosaurus mongoliensis is flat on top with a triangular depression called the antorbital fossa on the upper jaw bone.
facts.quote: Skulls of P. mongoliensis are flat on top, especially over the back of the skull, with a triangular depression, the antorbital fossa, on the outside surface of the maxilla

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus mongoliensis is considered one of the largest known species of Psittacosaurus.
facts.quote: P. mongoliensis is among the largest known species

facts.statement: The type specimen skull of Psittacosaurus mongoliensis measures 15.2 centimetres long and its associated femur is 16.2 centimetres long.
facts.quote: The skull of the type specimen, which is probably a juvenile, is 15.2 centimetres (6 in) long, and the associated femur is 16.2 centimetres (6.4 in) in length

facts.statement: The largest documented femur of Psittacosaurus mongoliensis measures about 21 centimetres long.
facts.quote: Other specimens are larger, with the largest documented femur measuring about 21 centimetres (8.25 in) long

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus sinensis is easily distinguished from other species by numerous unique skull features.
facts.quote: P. sinensis is readily distinguished from all other species by numerous features of the skull

facts.statement: The cheek bones of Psittacosaurus sinensis flare out to form horns that are proportionally wider than in any other species except P. sibiricus and P. lujiatunensis.
facts.quote: The jugals flare out sideways, forming 'horns' proportionally wider than in any other known Psittacosaurus species except P. sibiricus and P. lujiatunensis

facts.statement: Due to its flared cheek bones, the skull of Psittacosaurus sinensis is wider than it is long.
facts.quote: Because of the flared cheeks, the skull is actually wider than it is long

facts.statement: The lower jaw of Psittacosaurus sinensis lacks the hollow opening found in other species and bows outwards, creating an underbite appearance.
facts.quote: The mandible (lower jaw) lacks the hollow opening, or fenestra, seen in other species, and the entire lower jaw is bowed outwards, giving the animal the appearance of an underbite

facts.statement: The skull of an adult Psittacosaurus sinensis can reach 11.5 centimetres in length.
facts.quote: The skull of an adult P. sinensis can reach 11.5 centimeters (4.5 in) in length

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus sibiricus is the largest-known species of Psittacosaurus.
facts.quote: P. sibiricus is the largest-known species of Psittacosaurus

facts.statement: The type specimen of Psittacosaurus sibiricus has a skull 20.7 centimetres long and a femur 22.3 centimetres long.
facts.quote: The skull of the type specimen is 20.7 centimetres long (8.25 in), and the femur is 22.3 cm (8.75 in) in length

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus sibiricus has a neck frill longer than any other species, measuring 15 to 18% of skull length.
facts.quote: It is also distinguished by its neck frill, which is longer than any other species, at 15 to 18% of skull length

facts.statement: The cheek bone of Psittacosaurus sibiricus has extremely prominent horns that may contact the premaxilla, features also seen in P. sinensis.
facts.quote: The jugal has extremely prominent 'horns' and may contact the premaxilla, both features also seen in the possibly related P. sinensis

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus sibiricus has a flange on the lower jaw similar to that found in P. mongoliensis, P. meileyingensis, and P. sattayaraki.
facts.quote: There is a flange on the dentary of the lower jaw, similar to P. mongoliensis, P. meileyingensis, and P. sattayaraki

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus sibiricus can be distinguished from other species by a combination of 32 anatomical features, six of which are unique to it.
facts.quote: It can be told apart from the other species of Psittacosaurus by a combination of 32 anatomical features, including six that are unique to the species

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus xinjiangensis is distinguished by a prominent cheek horn flattened on the front end and specific tooth features.
facts.quote: P. xinjiangensis is distinguished by a prominent jugal 'horn' that is flattened on the front end, as well as some features of the teeth

facts.statement: The complete type skull of Psittacosaurus meileyingensis is 13.7 centimetres long.
facts.quote: The complete type skull, probably adult, is 13.7 centimetres (5.5 in) long

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus neimongoliensis has a distinctly narrow frontal bone, resulting in a narrower overall skull.
facts.quote: The frontal bone of P. neimongoliensis is distinctly narrow compared to that of other species, resulting in a narrower skull overall

facts.statement: In Psittacosaurus neimongoliensis, the ischium bone is longer than the femur, differing from other species.
facts.quote: The ischium bone of the pelvis is also longer than the femur, which differs from other species in which these bones are known

facts.statement: The type specimen of Psittacosaurus neimongoliensis has a skull length of 13.2 centimetres and a femur length of 13 centimetres, though it was not fully grown.
facts.quote: The type specimen has a skull length of 13.2 centimetres (5.2 in) and a femoral length of 13 centimetres (5.1 in), but is not fully grown

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus ordosensis is distinguished by numerous features of its cheek bones, which have very prominent horns.
facts.quote: P. ordosensis can be distinguished by numerous features of the jugals, which have very prominent 'horns'

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus ordosensis is the smallest known species of Psittacosaurus.
facts.quote: It is also the smallest known species

facts.statement: One adult skull of Psittacosaurus ordosensis measures only 9.5 centimetres in length.
facts.quote: One adult skull measures only 9.5 centimeters (3.75 in) in length

facts.statement: The type skull of Psittacosaurus lujiatunensis measures 19 centimetres long, while the largest known skull is 20.5 centimetres long.
facts.quote: The type skull of P. lujiatunensis measures 19 cm (7.5 in) in length, while the largest-known skull is 20.5 centimetres (8 in) long

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus lujiatunensis has a fossa in front of the eye, similar to P. mongoliensis.
facts.quote: There is a fossa in front of the eye, as in P. mongoliensis

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus mongoliensis was a contemporary of Psittacosaurus gobiensis.
facts.quote: P. mongoliensis was a contemporary

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus is the type genus of the family Psittacosauridae, a name established by Osborn in 1923.
facts.quote: Classification Psittacosaurus is the type genus of the family Psittacosauridae, which was also named by Osborn in 1923.

facts.statement: Psittacosaurids were positioned as basal to nearly all known ceratopsians, with the possible exceptions of Yinlong and the Chaoyangsauridae.
facts.quote: Psittacosaurids were basal to almost all known ceratopsians except Yinlong and perhaps the Chaoyangsauridae.

facts.statement: Unlike other ceratopsians that retained five hand digits, all species of Psittacosaurus possessed only four digits on each hand.
facts.quote: All other ceratopsians retained the fifth digit of the hand, a plesiomorphy or primitive trait, whereas all species of Psittacosaurus had only four digits on the hand.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analysis suggests that the ceratopsian group likely originated in Asia, as most taxa outside specific families are found there.
facts.quote: The authors (Farke et al.) noted that all taxa outside of Leptoceratopsidae and Coronosauria with the exception of their genus Aquilops are from Asia, meaning the group likely originated there.

facts.statement: There is currently no scientific consensus regarding the relationships between the many named species of Psittacosaurus.
facts.quote: Although many species of Psittacosaurus have been named, their relationships to each other have not yet been fully explored and no scientific consensus exists on the subject.

facts.statement: The encephalization quotient (EQ) of P. lujiatunensis is 0.31, which is significantly higher than that of genera like Triceratops.
facts.quote: The EQ score for P. lujiatunensis is 0.31, significantly higher than genera such as Triceratops.

facts.statement: A higher encephalization quotient correlates with more complex behavior, a trait seen in various dinosaurs and birds with EQs ranging from 0.36 to 2.98.
facts.quote: A higher EQ correlates with more complex behaviour, and various dinosaurs have high EQs, similar to birds, which range from 0.36 to 2.98.

facts.statement: Behaviors such as nest-building, parental care, and bird-like sleeping, associated with high EQs, have been observed in Psittacosaurus.
facts.quote: Behaviours influenced by high EQs include nest-building, parental care, and bird-like sleeping, some of which have been shown to be present in Psittacosaurus.

facts.statement: The presence of large olfactory bulbs indicates that Psittacosaurus possessed an acute sense of smell.
facts.quote: Large olfactory bulbs are present, indicating the genus had an acute sense of smell.

facts.statement: Large, curved semicircular canals indicate that Psittacosaurus was much more agile than later ceratopsians.
facts.quote: The curvature of the semicircular canals is related to the agility of reptiles, and the large curved canals in Psittacosaurus show that the genus was much more agile than later ceratopsians.

facts.statement: Comparisons with modern birds and reptiles suggest Psittacosaurus may have been cathemeral, active both day and night.
facts.quote: Comparisons between the scleral rings of Psittacosaurus and modern birds and reptiles suggest that it may have been cathemeral, active throughout the day and for short intervals at night.

facts.statement: Research suggests that while some Psittacosaurus species were semi-aquatic, others were more terrestrial.
facts.quote: They further suggested that some species of Psittacosaurus were more terrestrial than others.

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus possessed self-sharpening teeth adapted for cropping and slicing tough plant material.
facts.quote: Psittacosaurs had self-sharpening teeth that would have been useful for cropping and slicing tough plant material.

facts.statement: Unlike later ceratopsians, Psittacosaurus lacked teeth suitable for grinding or chewing food.
facts.quote: Unlike later ceratopsians, they did not have teeth suitable for grinding or chewing their food.

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus used gastroliths, stones swallowed to aid in breaking down food within the digestive system.
facts.quote: Instead, they used gastroliths—stones swallowed to wear down food as it passed through the digestive system.

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus possessed akinetic skulls where the upper and lower jaws functioned as single units without internal joints.
facts.quote: Unlike many other dinosaurs, psittacosaurs had akinetic skulls: that is to say, the upper and lower jaws each behaved as a single unit, without internal joints.

facts.statement: The beaks of Psittacosaurus were rounded and flattened rather than forming the curved tips seen in most ceratopsians.
facts.quote: Unlike most ceratopsians, their beaks did not form curved tips, but were instead rounded and flattened.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Psittacosaurus jaws may have served a nutcracking function when the lower beak was retracted inside the upper beak.
facts.quote: If the jaws were aligned, the beaks could be used to crop objects, but if the lower jaw was retracted so that the lower beak was inside the upper beak, the jaws may have served a nutcracking function.

facts.statement: The presence of gastroliths in well-preserved skeletons suggests Psittacosaurus likely had a diet rich in nuts or seeds.
facts.quote: A nut- or seed-rich diet would also match well with the gastroliths often seen in well-preserved psittacosaur skeletons.

facts.statement: Phil Senter suggested that if Psittacosaurus needed to dig depressions in the ground, it likely used its hindlimbs instead of its forelimbs.
facts.quote: The forelimbs were also too short to be used in digging or bringing food to the mouth, and Senter suggested that if Psittacosaurus found it necessary to dig depressions in the ground it may have used its hindlimbs instead.

facts.statement: Despite their limited reach, Psittacosaurus hands may have been used to carry nesting material or food to specific locations.
facts.quote: Even though the hands could not reach the mouth, Psittacosaurus could have still used them to carry nesting material or food to a desired location.

facts.statement: Research by Qi Zhao from the University of Bristol on 16 specimens suggests Psittacosaurus was probably secondarily bipedal, not bipedal for its entire lifespan.
facts.quote: However, Psittacosaurus may not have been entirely bipedal for its entire lifespan. Taking sections from the limb bones of 16 specimens of Psittacosaurus, ranging in age from less than a year old to ten-year-old adults, Qi Zhao from the University of Bristol found that Psittacosaurus was probably secondarily bipedal.

facts.statement: Infant Psittacosaurus grew their front limbs faster than their hind limbs between hatching and three years of age.
facts.quote: The infants' front limbs grew at faster rates than the hind limbs at between hatching and three years of age.

facts.statement: Between four and six years of age, Psittacosaurus arm growth slowed while leg growth accelerated as the animal matured.
facts.quote: At the age of between four and six years, arm growth slowed and leg growth accelerated as the animal became mature.

facts.statement: Evidence suggests the ancestor of Psittacosaurus was quadrupedal and that young individuals retained this gait while adults evolved to be bipedal.
facts.quote: These findings further reveal that the ancestor of Psittacosaurus was likely quadrupedal and eventually gained the ability to become bipedal as it evolved, with the young retaining the quadrupedal gait of the ancestor in question.

facts.statement: The smallest known Psittacosaurus is a P. mongoliensis hatchling at the AMNH measuring only 11 to 13 centimetres long with a 2.4 cm skull.
facts.quote: The smallest is a P. mongoliensis hatchling conserved in the American Museum of Natural History (AMNH), which is only 11 to 13 centimetres (4–5 inches) long, with a skull 2.4 cm in length.

facts.statement: Histological studies show P. mongoliensis grew from less than 1 kg at three years old to almost 20 kg at nine years old.
facts.quote: A histological examination of P. mongoliensis has determined the growth rate of these animals. The smallest specimens in the study were estimated at three years old and less than 1 kg, while the largest were nine years old and weighed almost 20 kg.

facts.statement: Growth ring counts suggest the maximum longevity of P. mongoliensis was 10 to 11 years.
facts.quote: An age determination study performed on the fossilized remains of P. mongoliensis by using growth ring counts suggest that the longevity of the basal ceratopsian was 10 to 11 years.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence of a mixed-age herd of six individuals buried together provides the earliest known evidence of gregarious behavior in any ceratopsian dinosaur.
facts.quote: The find of a herd of six Psittacosaurus individuals killed and buried by a volcanic mudflow indicates the presence of at least two age groups from two distinct clutches gathered together.

facts.statement: A 2025 discovery of 13 juvenile skeletons, each containing gastroliths, suggests these young dinosaurs swallowed stones to aid digestion.
facts.quote: In 2025, Wang and colleagues reported a specimen consisting of 13 juvenile Psittacosaurus skeletons (JLU DERC-Z0007), with nearly every individual containing gastroliths.

facts.statement: A fossil containing a juvenile Psittacosaurus inside the stomach of a large mammal represents the first known example of a Mesozoic mammal preying on a live dinosaur.
facts.quote: One skeleton of Repenomamus robustus, a large triconodont mammal, is preserved with the remains of a juvenile Psittacosaurus in its abdominal cavity.

facts.statement: Scientists hypothesize that heavy predation on juveniles led to R-selection, where the species produced many offspring to offset high mortality.
facts.quote: Heavy predation on juvenile Psittacosaurus may have resulted in R-selection, the production of more numerous offspring to counteract this loss.

facts.statement: Psittacosaurus fossils are found exclusively in Early Cretaceous sediments across Asia, ranging from southern Siberia and northern China to possibly Thailand.
facts.quote: All Psittacosaurus fossils discovered so far have been found in Early Cretaceous sediments in Asia, from southern Siberia to northern China, and possibly as far south as Thailand.

facts.statement: Most Psittacosaurus fossils date to the late Barremian through Albian stages of the Early Cretaceous, approximately 125 to 105 million years ago.
facts.quote: The most common age of geologic formations bearing Psittacosaurus fossils is from the late Barremian through Albian stages of the Early Cretaceous, or approximately 125 to 105 mya (million years ago).

facts.statement: Argon-argon dating of the Yixian Formation suggests the lowest beds are about 128 million years old and the highest are approximately 122 million years old.
facts.quote: Using argon–argon dating, a team of Chinese scientists dated the lowest beds in the formation to about 128 mya, and the highest to approximately 122 mya.
